Hardware and software block diagrams, the finger tracking maps, and the verification results. Presented at the UTSA Tech Symposium, where the project took first place out of 89 teams.

docs.title: Magic Mitts: Verification, and what we actually proved
docs.text: Verification, and what we actually proved. We ran a formal verification and validation plan against the glove's core functions rather than demoing it and calling it done. Six test cases, all passed. ID What it verifies Result. TS-01. The electromagnetic system consistently applies force to restrict finger movement. Pass. TS-02. Haptic feedback provides accurate tactile feedback when virtual objects are touched. Pass. TS-03. Flex sensors accurately track the position and movement of each finger in real time. Pass. TS-04. The Bluetooth connection maintains stability, range and latency.

docs.title: Magic Mitts: Verification, and what we actually proved
docs.text: Pass. TS-05. Battery provides adequate usage time and remains operational during recharging. Pass. TS-06. The glove remains comfortable during prolonged wear and repeated use without significant damage. Pass. I want to be careful about what that table does and does not claim. It says the glove does what we designed it to do, repeatably, under test. It is not a controlled user study, and I am not going to dress it up as one. Comfort in TS-06 means it survived prolonged wear without damage or complaint from the people testing it, not a validated comfort score against a control.

docs.title: Magic Mitts: Engineering inside real constraints
docs.text: Engineering inside real constraints. The part of senior design that stuck with me was that the constraints document came before the fun part, and it was not busywork. Economic. The fifty dollar target was the whole thesis, so every component choice was a tradeoff against it. A decision matrix, not taste. Manufacturing. Assembling the glove requires sewing, which is not a widely held skillset in the US, so a design that assumed easy assembly would not have survived contact with production.

docs.title: Magic Mitts: Engineering inside real constraints
docs.text: Environmental. Material choices were weighed for sustainability rather than picked purely on performance. Schedule. Two semesters, fixed design reviews, and suppliers who do not care about your timeline. None of that is glamorous and all of it is why the thing existed by the deadline.

docs.title: Magic Mitts: My part in it
docs.text: My part in it. Four of us: two electrical engineers, two computer engineers. I led the team, and my hands-on work was the software and integration half, the Unity side and the embedded control, plus the interaction design decisions about what a given event should feel like and when. The integration seam is where most of the difficulty lived. A virtual collision has to become a decision about which finger, which response, and how long, and it has to arrive fast enough that a person reads it as the same event rather than as a consequence of one. Most of what I learned on this project was about that seam.

docs.title: Magic Mitts: What I would do differently
docs.text: What I would do differently. Measure properly, and pre-register what counts as success. The reason I had to pull two numbers off this page later is that we measured casually and wrote confidently. I would rather have three defensible numbers than six impressive ones. Run a real user study with a control condition. We had the hardware to do it and ran out of semester. Revisit the brake resolution. Fifty newtons of stop is a binary that convinces you a surface is there.

docs.title: Magic Mitts: What I would do differently
docs.text: Communicating how hard something is, rather than only that it exists, is the next problem and a much more interesting one. This project is also the direct ancestor of the Vision Pro work I did two years later. Same question about touch in immersive systems, opposite approach: instead of building hardware to put on the hand, use the hardware somebody is already wearing. All projects GitHub.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone
docs.text: Case study • iOS and Android • Design system and architecture. Ember: a week, then gone. A private photo app for a small circle of friends. Share a trip the way you would hand someone an album, let them pick what they want to look at, and then let it go. My first real UI project, and the one where I finally built a design system instead of just picking colours. Rabiat Sadiq 2026 iOS, Android, and a backend. Design system. Two-half palette, one typeface. Deletion. Three independent layers. Transfer. 1.5 MB where it would be 50.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: It starts with the name
docs.text: It starts with the name. Ember sits inside both of the words the product is made of. rem ember · m ember. A closed group of members, sharing things they will remember precisely because the photos did not stay. And an ember is literally what the product is: warm, alive for a while, and then not. Nothing in the naming had to be invented, which is usually the sign that a name is right. So the launch animation just shows you.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: It starts with the name
docs.text: The wordmark opens on remember in cursive, the re blurs and lifts away, then the m goes the same way, and you are left with ember as the mark dissolves into the feed. The whole thing is under two seconds, which is roughly a cold app launch anyway, so it costs the user nothing. It explains the name once, on first open, without a single line of onboarding copy.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The problem I actually wanted to solve
docs.text: The problem I actually wanted to solve. Your friends get back from a trip. They have two hundred photos and they want to share them with you and about nine other people. So what happens now. They send the same set to each person, one at a time. And every one of those sends is a copy. The original is on their phone. The version they sent you is stored again in that thread. The version they sent the next person is stored again in that thread.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The problem I actually wanted to solve
docs.text: Most people do not realise this, but the photos inside your messages are storage too, sitting on your device, counting against you. Multiply that across a friend group and everyone quietly runs out of space, holding many copies of the same trip. You still need to share with your friends. Social media is too public. So you are stuck choosing between the thing that eats your phone and the thing that tells everyone. The alternative I wanted was closer to a physical gesture.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The problem I actually wanted to solve
docs.text: You hand someone an album. They turn the pages and look at what they want to look at. They say something about the one they liked, either to you or to the whole room. And if there is one they really want, they take it. That is the interaction model. Not a feed. Not a broadcast. Showing your friends a dump and letting them choose what to see, react to it, and talk about it, one on one or as a group.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The problem I actually wanted to solve
docs.text: Which is where the fade comes from. A photo does not sit at full quality for seven days and vanish at a cliff. It loses resolution across its week, and near the end it lifts away into drifting specks of light. Press and hold and you see it whole again, for as long as you hold. What is left at the very end is the thirty six bytes of colour it arrived as. A hard cliff makes you check the clock.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The problem I actually wanted to solve
docs.text: A slow fade makes you look now. Keeping is deliberate on both sides: the poster allows it, the keeper chooses it, and the poster is told. Detail leaves first, colour last. At the end the bytes are deleted and the key destroyed. Replies are the conversation: text, ten second voice notes, GIFs, your own stickers. Circles set a standing day for themselves. Waffle Wednesday. Sunday Long Way Home. On its day the feed shows who has posted, and that is the entire nudge. There is no streak to protect, because obligation is what kills a group chat. The moment an app can punish you for not showing up, showing up stops meaning anything.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: The design system. This was my first real UI project, and I built it the year I was finishing MHCI, so it is also the place where I got to find out what I actually think about design rather than what I could recite. Everything below is a decision with a reason attached. If the code and the reason ever disagree, the code is wrong. The feeling I was aiming for is coming home. Not a product, a room. You are flipping through an album with people who were there, and when one of them is good you say so, and if one of them matters you keep it.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Warmth is not decoration here, it is the brief. The tokens live in Theme.swift and the reasoning lives beside them in the repo, so the two cannot drift. The same tokens are mirrored into a Figma library generated from the iOS source, so a value that disagrees between the two is a bug in one of them rather than a style choice. Five principles the whole thing hangs off. The photograph is the interface. Chrome sits on top of images inside glass, never stacked above and below them.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Where a shape can carry meaning it does: the countdown is a ring, the frame count is a stacked edge, a reaction is the sticker itself. Say it once, in as few words as possible. All interface copy is lowercase, under six words, and appears once. Recognition is faster than reading, and a small closed group does not need instructing, because a friend handed them the app. Time is a colour before it is a number. Mint means days, butter means the last fifth, coral means hours.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: The numeral is still there for anyone who wants it. Warm, not neutral. The background is #FDF8F4, not white. Ink is #1B1620, not black. The promise is visible. Storage, expiry and deletion are not settings screens. A claim you can watch working beats a paragraph in a privacy policy. Information hierarchy: the drop card. The single most important layout in the app, and the one I would put in front of a design review first. A typical photo-feed row spends about 90pt on metadata stacked above and below the image.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Ember spends about 34pt, placed on the photo itself, behind glass. That difference is not a detail. It is the difference between seeing one card on screen and seeing two. Everything on that card is ranked. The photograph is the content, so it keeps its own aspect ratio, clamped between 0.8 and 1.9 and capped at 380pt tall. The things you need at a glance, who posted and how long is left, sit on a glass bar over the bottom of the image.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: The caption is capped at two lines and truncates on purpose, because the card must not grow unbounded to accommodate someone who wrote an essay. Reactions and comment count sit outside the frame, below, because they are about the photo rather than part of it. Hierarchy is mostly deciding what is allowed to push everything else down the screen. White space, and having very few legal values. Spacing runs on a 4pt base with a deliberately short scale: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, and a screen margin of 20 that never changes on any screen, ever.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Nothing is edge to edge except a photograph in the viewer. Seven values is the entire vocabulary, and the shortness is the point. Most of what makes an interface feel untidy is one-off padding, someone nudging a thing four points to make one screen look right. You cannot write a one-off padding if the only values in scope are these seven. Constraint does the tidying so discipline does not have to. Corners are continuous rather than the default circular, at four sizes: 12 for chips, 18 for controls, 28 for cards, 36 for sheets.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Card radius is large deliberately. A big soft rectangle reads as a photographic object rather than a UI panel, and that is most of why the feed feels like a stack of prints instead of a list of posts. A palette in two halves. This is the decision I would defend hardest, because it is what stops a pastel interface from becoming unusable. The palette is split, and the halves have different jobs and different rules. Hue is the pastel half, used only for fills: backgrounds, gradients, avatar ramps, banner washes.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Large, low contrast, decorative, chosen purely for how they sit underneath a photograph. They carry no meaning, so they carry no contrast obligation. Every one is desaturated enough to sit under an image without competing with it. peach #FFB49A. coral #FF7E6B. lilac #C0B2F2. sky #9ED3F0. mint #9FE3C4. butter #FFDF9E. rose #F9AFC6. sage #BFDCA8. Signal is the deeper half, used only for meaning: the countdown ring, urgency, the kept state. Every one is held to a 3:1 contrast minimum, because if you cannot tell mint from coral then you cannot tell four days from four hours. fresh #2E9E72 · 3.19:1. fading #B8820F · 3.19:1. urgent #D9503C · 3.86:1. kept #7C6BE0 · 3.95:1.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: The example that made the rule concrete: pastel mint measures 1.40:1. As a background wash that is completely fine. As the colour telling you how long a memory has left, it is unusable. So the halves are separated in code, and nothing in the app may use a colour that is not a token. The ground is warm for a reason too. Pure neutrals next to peach read as holes punched in the page, and warm off-whites flatter skin tones, which is most of what gets photographed here.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: One typeface, and no custom font. The reflexive move for a consumer app is to licence a display face. I decided against it, and the reasoning is a good example of the system arguing with itself. Weight. A usable custom family runs 200 to 400 KB across its weights. On an app whose entire pitch is not hoarding bytes, that is an awkward first impression. Dynamic Type. iOS reflows the system faces correctly across the full accessibility range, in every script.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Custom faces need per-size optical work that almost never gets done, and it breaks first at the largest sizes, which is exactly where it matters most. Coverage. SF ships every script the app could need. A boutique face ships Latin. It is not where the brand lives. Ember is recognisable from the cursive mark, the pastel-on-paper palette, the countdown ring and the way it moves. None of that depends on the body face, so none of it breaks when Apple ships a new SF revision.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: So: SF Pro Rounded everywhere, with Snell Roundhand reserved for the wordmark. Rounded specifically, because softened terminals read as friendly without reading as childish, and they sit correctly beside a cursive letterform that is also soft-terminalled. Eight size tokens, all on Font.system so they scale automatically. I wrote down where it breaks under stress rather than pretending it does not: tab bar labels crowd first and should drop to symbols above AX2, and the expiry ring drops its numeral at accessibility sizes and lets the ring carry the meaning alone, with the full sentence still read aloud by VoiceOver.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Icons, and shapes instead of icons. SF Symbols, for the same reason as the type: they are on every device, they align optically to the text baseline for free, they inherit weight from the surrounding font, and they are what an iOS user already knows. A custom set would cost drawing time, add weight, and be less legible on day one. The set is small, and every symbol earns its place by appearing in more than one context or by having no shape alternative.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Where a shape is a better answer than a symbol, the shape wins: the countdown is a ring, not a clock glyph, and the frame count is a stacked edge on the card, not a number in a badge. Voice. Lowercase, short, and never explaining itself. This is the part people skip and it is half of how an interface feels. Ember says Not. gone in. Select an expiration duration. add yours. Participate in today's prompt. nothing burning. You have no active posts. say something before it goes.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Be the first to comment! kept. maya will see. Photo saved to your library. Motion has one rule. Motion explains where something came from, or it does not happen. A sheet rises from the button that opened it. A sticker scales up from the point you tapped. A card fades and lifts three percent on first appearance so a feed assembles rather than snapping. Nothing spins, bounces or slides purely to be noticed. Everything is one of two families, which is why transitions across the app feel related.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: Settle is springs, for anything a finger caused, tuned so the element arrives just after the finger leaves. That small lag is what makes an interface feel physical instead of laggy. Reveal is eased curves, for anything the app did on its own. Exactly one curve overshoots, reserved for stickers and reactions, where a bit of bounce is the entire emotional payload. Using it anywhere else would spend the effect. Circles, each with its own standing day. Audience and lifespan are chosen per drop, not per account.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The design system
docs.text: The feed. Chrome on the photo, not stacked around it. Accessibility is in the system, not bolted on. Anything interactive is at least 44 by 44 points regardless of how small the glyph inside it looks. Dynamic Type is supported across the full accessibility range, which is most of why there is no custom font. Meaningful colour is held to a contrast floor while decorative colour is not, which is the whole reason the palette is split. And anywhere colour carries state, a number or a spoken sentence carries it too, so the ring is never the only way to know how long you have.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The backend, and why I pushed on it so hard
docs.text: The backend, and why I pushed on it so hard. I want to be accurate about this rather than modest about it. The design and the architecture were equally important, and they took roughly equal amounts of care. But I was deliberate about wanting the backend to be as strong as I could make it, because photos are finicky and the failure modes are all miserable. You do not want to lose someone's image. You do not want it stored in the wrong place.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The backend, and why I pushed on it so hard
docs.text: You do not want a permission check that quietly lets the wrong person see something, or one that locks a member out of their own circle. And unusually for a photo app, this one is supposed to destroy things on a schedule, which means a bug in the wrong direction deletes something early and a bug in the other direction breaks the entire promise. The whole product is a technical claim. "It goes away" is not something you can express in a layout.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The backend, and why I pushed on it so hard
docs.text: If deletion is soft, or recoverable, or depends on my application code being correct, then the app is lying and the interface is decoration on top of a lie. So the architecture had to be true first, and then the design had somewhere honest to stand. Figure 1. The architecture, and the part of it that actually carries the promise. What "its own key" means, in plain words. Encryption words get thrown around, so here is what is actually happening.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The backend, and why I pushed on it so hard
docs.text: Every drop gets its own private key, generated on the phone, used for nothing else. The photo is locked with that key before it ever leaves the device, using AES-256-GCM, which is the standard lock that also tells you if someone tampered with the box. So what travels to the server is a sealed box, and the server never receives the key that opens it. Then the key has to reach the right people and nobody else. Each member of the circle has their own public and private key pair.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The backend, and why I pushed on it so hard
docs.text: The drop's key is put in a small envelope addressed to each member individually, locked with their public key, using X25519. Six people in the circle means six envelopes. Each person can open exactly their own envelope, get the drop key, and unlock the photo. Anyone else holds an envelope they cannot open, and the server holds a box it cannot open. Which is what makes the expiry real. Destroying the drop key is not a flag in a database saying "deleted."

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The backend, and why I pushed on it so hard
docs.text: It removes the only thing that could ever turn those bytes back into a picture. Whatever survives, wherever it survived, is noise. There is a test for exactly that, and it is the most important test in the project: seal a photo, store it, read it back successfully, shred the key, read again. Nothing comes out. That test is the product. None of that is hidden from the user either. The app ships with a fine print screen that explains what happens to your photos, who can see you, and what is kept, in the same plain language as above. Being able to read the actual promise from inside the app, rather than finding it in a policy document nobody opens, is the point. Transparency is a feature here, not a compliance step.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The storage thesis
docs.text: The storage thesis. Ephemerality is usually framed as a privacy feature. It is also an economics feature, and that is the half that makes the app possible for one person to run. A photo app that keeps everything forever has a cost curve that only goes up, which is why every one of them eventually sells you storage or sells your attention. If content expires by design, storage cost stops compounding. Running this for a friend group today costs the ninety nine dollar developer program fee and nothing else, because the free database tier is genuinely enough when nothing accumulates.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The storage thesis
docs.text: On top of that, every photo becomes three renditions and the app is careful about which one it asks for. Rendition Long edge Fetched when. thumb. 400px. Every card, always cached. display. 2048px. A photo goes full screen. original. Untouched. A pinch to zoom, or a keep. Six friends browsing a ten photo drop move about 1.5 MB, not 50 MB, and still get the untouched file the instant somebody actually wants it. Quality is never lost, only deferred. And as a drop ages the larger renditions are deleted first, so most of its storage is released long before the drop itself is.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: The storage thesis
docs.text: Which brings it back to where this started. One copy, shared with the people you chose, that cleans up after itself. Instead of ten copies in ten threads that never do. Shown, not claimed. The profile screen tells you how many bytes you are actually holding and how many have already been released. If the thesis is that this app stays small, the number belongs on screen.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: Both platforms, one promise
docs.text: Both platforms, one promise. iPhone is SwiftUI. Android is Expo, built in the cloud with EAS. Same server, same crypto: a drop sealed on an iPhone opens on Android, and that is proven by a parity test running against a vector the Swift tests emit, rather than by me assuming two implementations of the same spec agree. The app boots into a seeded world with four circles, a live Waffle Wednesday, and a drop in its final hours, so the states that are hard to reach are always one launch away.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: Both platforms, one promise
docs.text: Without a server configured it runs entirely on device, and the profile screen tells you which mode you are in. Tests cover the media pipeline, sealing, key wrapping, shredding, the decay ladder and the models, plus UI tests for the flows that break silently. There is also a suite that runs the real client against the real project, which is how a client and a schema that quietly disagree get caught. It found four real bugs the first time it ran.

docs.title: Ember: a week, then gone: What I would do next
docs.text: What I would do next. Run it with an actual circle of friends for a month. Everything above is a design argument until a group of people either keeps opening it or does not. Watch whether the fade reads as intended or as a bug. Losing detail on purpose is the riskiest idea in the product and the one most likely to be misread. Work out whether keeps stay rare. If everyone keeps everything, the app quietly becomes the archive I was trying not to build. All projects GitHub.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing
docs.text: CMU MHCI • UCRE • Fall 2025. The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing. Can ordinary people spot harmful behaviour in generative AI, and would they report it if they did? Our team started with Meta AI across Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger and Quest, then tested that question on real data and a real auditing tool: CMU's WeAudit survey and its TAIGA platform. When. Sep to Oct 2025. My role. Lead Researcher, team of 5. Methods. Background research • Data analysis • Heuristic evaluation • Usability testing.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: The question
docs.text: The question. This was Project 1 of User-Centered Research and Evaluation (05-610), "Learning From What Exists". We started broad, asking how Meta uses generative AI across its platforms, with a goal that stayed the same all project: how can we empower and incentivize everyday users to understand, identify and report harmful algorithmic behaviours? Sep 2025 Background research on Meta AI. Sep 28 Data analysis report on the WeAudit bias survey. Oct 2 to 5 Heuristic evaluation of WeAudit TAIGA, individual then as a team. Oct 12 Usability testing: 10 moderated sessions and findings.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 1. Background research: living with Meta AI
docs.text: 1. Background research: living with Meta AI. Each of us did two hands-on sessions with Meta AI (celebrity and "mind reader" chatbots on Instagram, WhatsApp trip planning, Messenger text and image generation, meta.ai, and Meta AI on Quest) and five informational reviews of news, research, Reddit threads and Meta's own documentation. That added up to ten experiential sessions and more than twenty sources. The bots blur who is human. A "Justin Bieber" bot kept insisting it was the real person.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 1. Background research: living with Meta AI
docs.text: A "Your Therapist" bot reported on Reddit claimed to be a licensed psychologist, complete with a fake licence number. Safety help is inconsistent. In our tests, crisis prompts were redirected to hotlines. In a Common Sense Media study with teen accounts, reported by the Washington Post, only about 1 in 5 harmful chats triggered any intervention. Privacy notices come late. WhatsApp told us Meta AI remembers chat details only after we had already shared some, and US users cannot opt out of their data being used for training.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 1. Background research: living with Meta AI
docs.text: The outputs carry stereotypes. Asked to imagine doctors and nurses, Messenger AI showed mostly young men as doctors, women only as nurses, and little racial diversity. The only feedback option was a downvote with a short list of reasons. Policy and experience don't match. Meta documents labels, memory controls and safeguards, but in everyday use they were easy to miss and applied unevenly. The thread through all of it: people can't report a harm they can't see, and the reporting tools that exist are too thin to capture what they do see.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 2. Data analysis: who sees bias as harm?
docs.text: 2. Data analysis: who sees bias as harm? Next we analysed survey data from WeAudit, a CMU HCII project, where participants rated how harmful AI-generated images were across race, gender and sexuality bias, then shared their demographics and their own experiences with discrimination. We built the analysis in Python (Pandas, NumPy, Plotly, Matplotlib in Google Colab). Recognition of harm was highest for race (about 65%) and gender (about 59%), much lower for sexuality (about 32%), and near zero for the neutral control.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 2. Data analysis: who sees bias as harm?
docs.text: Perceived harm is intersectional. The gap between the highest (non-binary participants, bias against Black/African American people, 6.1 of 7) and the lowest (male participants, bias against white people, 3.1) is 3 full points. Lived experience matters. People who had faced discrimination rated every kind of bias as more harmful, most of all racial bias, and the differences were statistically significant. Representation is the main reason. Missing or excluded groups were the most common justification for calling an image harmful, with more than 5,000 mentions in the open-text answers.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 2. Data analysis: who sees bias as harm?
docs.text: No partisan divide. Mapping mean scores by state, split by the 2020 election result and leaving out states with fewer than 20 participants, showed similar racial bias perception in Republican and Democratic states. Themes coded from open-text answers after stopword removal and tokenisation. Representation and diversity dominate the reasons for calling bias harmful. What it meant for the project: audits should prioritise race and gender, recruit diverse participants on purpose, and can frame racial bias as a shared concern rather than a polarising one.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 3. Heuristic evaluation: WeAudit TAIGA
docs.text: 3. Heuristic evaluation: WeAudit TAIGA. TAIGA is WeAudit's tool for the public to generate images with Stable Diffusion, compare outputs side by side and discuss bias in a forum. Each of us evaluated it against Nielsen's heuristics before we synthesised as a team. I focused on the discussion forum and on mobile, where content overflowed the screen and controls like reply buttons became hard to reach. Help and documentation: all five reviewers found nothing explaining how to prompt, compare or post.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 3. Heuristic evaluation: WeAudit TAIGA
docs.text: Consistency and standards: the Home link worked on some pages and not others. User control and freedom: a magnifier could trap you, and the prompt page had no way back. Error prevention: random characters still produced images, and new posts went up with no guidance. The strengths were real too: clear loading feedback, saved prompt history and a clean layout.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 4. Usability testing: 10 sessions
docs.text: 4. Usability testing: 10 sessions. We ran 10 moderated, think-aloud sessions with adults who use AI tools but had never seen TAIGA, and I ran two of them. Each person scanned the homepage, generated single and compared images, found their way home, and replied in the forum. We then clustered the transcripts by theme. Critical: nobody could tell what the site was for. All 10 participants were confused about its purpose, and the confusion lasted the whole session. The compare tool was misread.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 4. Usability testing: 10 sessions
docs.text: Three thought it compared two AI models. Everyone typed prompts unrelated to bias (birds, dogs), and nobody commented on bias in the results. Navigation failed. The logo didn't go home for 7 of 10, the hamburger menu did nothing for 5, and 8 missed the "Go to discussion forum" button. Quality undercut trust. Six called the images scary, inaccurate or useless, which made the audit itself feel pointless. What worked: five praised how fast images appeared, and many said auditing AI is something the public should care about.

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: 4. Usability testing: 10 sessions
docs.text: "I'm not sure, it doesn't really say what it's for; it just gives a place to type and generate something.". Our recommendations: global navigation with a working logo, a short optional walkthrough, "?" help beside Generate, Compare and Discuss, prompt inspiration shown by default, and a visible four-step flow (generate, analyse, give feedback, discuss).

docs.title: The Ethics of Meta: Everyday AI Auditing: What we learned
docs.text: What we learned. The project ended with a sharper answer about what everyday auditing needs: Agency needs usability. If people can't work the tool, they can't critique the AI. Agency needs a credible system. Bad outputs make auditing feel pointless. Agency needs a guided workflow. Without "what to do next", auditing becomes button-clicking. Responsiveness keeps people curious. Fast feedback kept participants experimenting. Plain language moves people. Participants wanted the site to talk about harm directly. My role was Lead Researcher: guiding the research, finding sources for the team and helping analyse the data. The same course's second project became my Spotify vs AI study.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark
docs.text: Essay • Lantern • Why I built it. If AI Goes Dark. Lantern is a language model that lives entirely on the phone. No server, no account, no signal needed. This is about why I wanted one, and about the object it is named after. Rabiat Sadiq September 2026 About a 7 minute read. Back home in Nigeria the light went out often. Not occasionally. Often. If the flashlight had not been charged, you had nothing. But there was always a lantern, and the lantern always worked.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark
docs.text: I have not seen one in a long time and I still think about it, because it is the clearest picture I have of what a dependable tool is. It does not need the grid. It does not need permission. It is small, it is yours, and it is enough for the thing you actually need to do right now, which is see.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: The worry that started it
docs.text: The worry that started it. A lot of people are concerned about AI, and a lot of the concern is fair. I am not going to litigate all of it here. The part that has been sitting with me is the power. The models we use every day run in buildings that burn an enormous amount of energy, mostly to stay cool, and every question you type gets routed to one of those buildings and back. That is true whether you asked it to summarise a contract or to fix the tone of a two line email.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: The worry that started it
docs.text: Side note My complete thought on that problem is here. It is ten seconds long and I stand by it. So I started wondering what it would be like to have something downloaded. Locally. On the thing in your pocket. Not as a political statement, just as a question: can the small tasks stay small?

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: The phone can do this now
docs.text: The phone can do this now. The honest answer a couple of years ago was no. The honest answer now is yes, for a surprising amount. The GPUs in the newer Pro phones are genuinely capable, Apple's unified memory means the model does not have to be copied around, and a quantised model of a billion or three billion parameters fits and runs at a speed that feels like typing. That covers more than you would think. Write an email.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: The phone can do this now
docs.text: Rewrite this so it is clearer. What is a word for this. Explain what this term means. Walk me through the first aid for this. None of those need a data center. They need something small, close, and available. Leave the big tasks to the big machines and let the little ones live on the phone. I need a little something. I do not have Google. I do not have anything. What can I ask? That last one is the situation I keep coming back to.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: The phone can do this now
docs.text: You are outside. You are stuck. There is no signal, or you are somewhere the signal is not yours to use. You need a small answer and you need it now. An on the go model that anyone can open at any time, with no connection, is a real thing that could exist, and as far as I can tell not many people have it yet. It will get better over time. It is already useful.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: What it is
docs.text: What it is. Lantern runs a quantised model entirely on the iPhone through MLX. The only network call it ever makes is the one time download of public model weights. After that it works in airplane mode, and the screen shows what that costs while it writes: tokens per second, memory in use, thermal state, live. The chat. "Ask anything. No signal needed." The readout underneath is the honest part. How Lantern works, in plain words. If it is going to live on your phone, you should know what it is doing there.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: What it is
docs.text: What staying on the phone has saved, with the assumptions behind the estimate spelled out. The part I am most careful about is the gate. Before anything downloads, the app reads the phone's memory, how much this process is still allowed to allocate, free disk, and whether the GPU is present, and then tells you per model: go, go with a warning, or not on this phone. A small model is the default and runs on four gigabyte phones. Bigger ones are offered with warnings where they belong and not at all where they would just crash. A lantern that sets your house on fire is not a lantern.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: Learning by building
docs.text: Learning by building. I will be straight about the other reason this exists. I got a new MacBook, I have been learning MLX and reading everything I can find about on device models, and this is how I learn: I make the thing. Reading about quantisation and reading about memory pressure is one kind of knowing. Watching a three billion parameter model get killed on a six gigabyte phone because I let the context grow is a different kind, and it is the kind that sticks. Lantern is one of those projects. It is me finding out what the phone can actually hold, and it will keep changing as I keep learning.

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: The name
docs.text: The name. A lantern is what you reach for when the light goes out. It does not care why it went out. It does not care whether the grid is overloaded or the bill was not paid or a storm took the line. It works because it is yours and it is already in the house. So the question the app is really asking is this. If, for whatever reason, AI goes dark, the service is down, the connection is gone, the price goes up, the policy changes, the building overheats, what could be our lantern?

docs.title: If AI Goes Dark: The name
docs.text: What is the small, dependable version that is already on the phone and does not need anyone's permission to turn on? We have a lot of devices now. They are not scarce any more. The open question, and I do not think it is settled, is whether we really have to run enormous centers and burn that much heat to answer questions that a thing in your pocket could answer on its own. I am going to keep learning and keep finding out what the devices can do. This one is a light. It is small. It works when nothing else does. Field Notes GitHub.

docs.title: Sillage
docs.text: Essay • No project attached • Perfume, music, and small things. Sillage. Sillage is the perfume word for the trail a scent leaves after the person has walked past. It is the part of a fragrance that other people experience and the wearer never does. This is about what software would look like if a perfumer designed it, and about why I keep building things that fade. Rabiat Sadiq August 2026 About a 10 minute read. A friend once called me from a building I had just left.

docs.title: Sillage
docs.text: Were you just in the elevator? I could smell your perfume. I had not been in that elevator for ten minutes. I think about that call more than it deserves. I was already gone. The scent was still doing something, to someone, on my behalf, and I would never know how it landed. That is sillage, and it turns out to be the thing I care most about in everything I make.

docs.title: Sillage: Everything is little things
docs.text: Everything is little things. Start with the boring truth about perfume: it is a bunch of small scents combined until they make one thing. Music is the same. One song is a bunch of small sounds, and if you go a layer down each sound is a bunch of frequencies, and a layer under that each frequency is a bunch of amplitudes, and under that it is just a lot of very small things. You can keep going. It does not stop being true.

docs.title: Sillage: Everything is little things
docs.text: A function in code is the same idea with a different name. Everything I have ever built is layers of something smaller. This is also, honestly, how I solve problems. If a problem is big, I make a smaller one out of it. If that one is still too big, smaller again, until it is so small that fixing it is obvious, and then I climb back up. It is how I learned to program. It is how I learned what a function even was.

docs.title: Sillage: Everything is little things
docs.text: It is a crucial part of how I live, and I did not notice until recently that it is also how a perfumer works, and how a producer layers a track, and how nature does almost everything. I keep finding biomimicry in places I did not put it. Break it down until it is easy. Then build it back up. Perfume, music, code.

docs.title: Sillage: What I wear, and why it is mine
docs.text: What I wear, and why it is mine. I wear what I feel like wearing. What I like will not be what you like, and I think that is one of the most interesting facts about people. We all arrive on earth as more or less nothing, the same nothing, and then we grow into something that is only ours. It shows up in handwriting, in how you walk, in how you write code, in what music you can stand.

docs.title: Sillage: What I wear, and why it is mine
docs.text: We are all essentially the same and all essentially unique at the same time, and perfume is the most intimate version of that I know. So I am chaotic about it, and the people who know me know this. Some days I want something simple and clean. Some days flowery. Some days unisex, some days something that reads as masculine. I have a decent array now. My sister taught me most of what I know, and I started where a lot of people start, with Carolina Herrera, and moved through Libre and a lot of others from there.

docs.title: Sillage: What I wear, and why it is mine
docs.text: Kayali is a house I follow closely. Their juicy apple layered with their pistachio is one of the best combinations I have found, and I am going to keep claiming I invented it until someone proves otherwise. Side note I almost never wear one scent. I put on two and find out what they make together, and I have discovered things I love that way that neither bottle would have given me alone. Some days I just want to be vanilla, so I wear vanilla in three different shades of vanilla.

docs.title: Sillage: What I wear, and why it is mine
docs.text: Why not. Layering again. It is always layering. I do not spend much on things. If I am going to slip, it will be on perfume or on technology, and I am at peace with that. Perfume is intimate in a way most purchases are not. It is the closest thing to you all day. There are tricks, too: a little Vaseline on the skin before you spray and it holds for hours longer. But mostly the answer is to buy the one that lasts, which brings me to the trade-off, and I will get there.

docs.title: Sillage: Reading other people's trails
docs.text: Reading other people's trails. I can walk into a room and know my sister was in it. Everyone has their own scent, and sometimes I walk into a place and think, this reminds me of someone, and then, this reminds me of a time. Smell files things by person and by period without asking you. Can I read a stranger from their sillage? A little. There is a particular masculine scent I can pick out on men that tells me something about who they are hoping to run into.

docs.title: Sillage: Reading other people's trails
docs.text: Mostly what it tells me is whether they know anything about perfume, because if I can name what someone is wearing we can have a conversation about it. That is a good one, I will say, or, you should try it with this. People are sometimes surprised that I know. Other people think it is common knowledge. Both reactions tell me something.

docs.title: Sillage: Interfaces have a smell
docs.text: Interfaces have a smell. When I was taking my fundamentals of interaction class, I kept reaching for scent to explain things to myself, and I think it holds up. Walk into a room and you can smell that it is clean before you have looked at anything. Walk into an Abercrombie and you are hit with the store's own perfume, sprayed on purpose, and Victoria's Secret does the same. The brand has an essence it is trying to give off, and it gets to you before a single word does.

docs.title: Sillage: Interfaces have a smell
docs.text: Interfaces work exactly like that. You can tell something is clean. You can tell something is smooth, or pastel, or sharp, or bubbly, before you have read a label or pressed a button. You eat with your eyes, people say, and it is true of a website. But you also eat with your nose: if the food smells off you do not want it, and biology put that reflex in front of your thinking on purpose, so that spoiled things get rejected before you have to reason about them.

docs.title: Sillage: Interfaces have a smell
docs.text: An interface gives off a smell in the first half second, and whatever it is, the user has already decided something. Side note There is a famous experiment where people are shown two shapes, one spiky and one round, and asked which is called Kiki and which is called Bouba. Almost everyone says the spiky one is Kiki. Nobody taught them that. We feel shapes the way we smell rooms, and design is just a way of choosing what people feel before they think.

docs.title: Sillage: Interfaces have a smell
docs.text: Figure 1. A perfume is designed in time. Something has to be bright and gone, something has to hold, and something has to still be there tomorrow. The shaded part is the point: after a few hours the wearer cannot smell it any more, and from then on it exists only for other people.

docs.title: Sillage: Designed to fade
docs.text: Designed to fade. Here is the thing perfumers know that software people mostly do not: you design in time. A scent has top notes that are bright and gone within the hour, heart notes that hold for the afternoon, and base notes that are still on your coat the next morning. The entire craft is deciding what fades when. Nothing in a good perfume is meant to last forever, and that is the design, not a limitation of it. I have been asked why I keep making things that go away, when the whole industry is built on things that pile up.

docs.title: Sillage: Designed to fade
docs.text: Accumulation is fine. It is also a kind of hoarding. People want to keep every image and every message, and it all takes space, and space costs money, and eventually it costs convenience too. Think about a Polaroid. You take one picture. You hand it to a friend, they look, they hand it back. You show the next person, and the next, seven people if you like. At the end you still have one photograph and seven people have seen it, and it cost you nothing to show them.

docs.title: Sillage: Designed to fade
docs.text: Digital broke that. Now, to show seven friends the same picture, I send it seven times and there are seven copies of it living on seven phones, and mine, and the act of showing someone something has quietly started costing storage, which is to say money. Ember exists because I wanted the Polaroid back. Show it to the people you chose, let them look, let it go. A perfumer would understand that immediately. Of course it fades. What did you think it was for?

docs.title: Sillage: Designed to fade
docs.text: Side note The one time someone tried to put actual smell into software, as far as I found, it did not go well. A game studio, I could not tell you which one now, worked on a device that would release scent to match what was on screen: flowers when you walked through a field, pizza when you saw pizza. It ran on a few chemicals mixed in a cartridge, and over time the cartridge just started to smell bad.

docs.title: Sillage: Designed to fade
docs.text: Every combination decayed toward the same off smell. There is probably a lesson in there about mixing things that were never meant to sit together in one box, but I mostly find it funny. Somebody built a fart machine by accident while chasing the flower field.

docs.title: Sillage: The trade-off is the same one
docs.text: The trade-off is the same one. What I dislike about how perfume is sold is the price, and the honest answer to the price is that you can usually get the same scent for a lot less, and it will not last as long. That is the trade. Longevity or cost. Pick. Which is exactly the shape of every trade I make at work. Overfit or underfit. Bias or variance. Storage or the ability to look at the photo forever.

docs.title: Sillage: The trade-off is the same one
docs.text: Privacy or convenience. There is no version of a system where you get all of it, and a lot of what I would call taste, in perfume or in engineering, is just knowing which side you are willing to lose on, and being honest that you chose it.

docs.title: Sillage: So, what would a perfumer build?
docs.text: So, what would a perfumer build? Something layered from small parts that each do one thing, the way a scent is built from notes and a song from sounds. Something with a shape in time: a bright opening that gets out of the way, a middle that holds, and a base you only notice once you have stopped looking. Something that leaves a trail you never see yourself, in what other people say about it after they close it. And something that fades on purpose, because a thing designed to last forever was never really designed at all. I was gone from that elevator for ten minutes. The best thing I could hope for anything I make is that it keeps working on someone after I have left the room. Field Notes.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn
docs.text: Essay • How we train AI • A thought in progress. The Point Was to Learn. We train AI by rewarding the finished task and hoping the learning comes along. Most of us grew up under the same deal. This summer, at OpenAI, the gap between the two showed up at a scale nobody planned for. What would it look like to reward the learning instead? Rabiat Sadiq October 2026 About a 16 minute read. Somewhere while growing up, most of us pick up a second skill alongside whatever we are meant to be learning.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn
docs.text: We learn the test. Which formula always comes up, what the grader wants to see, which questions repeat from year to year, how to sound sure of an answer we only half follow. Nobody teaches it. It gets absorbed, because it pays. It reaches well past school. The language you can pass an exam in and still not order lunch in. The interview you get through on rehearsed answers. The team whose number on the dashboard keeps climbing while the work it was meant to track stays where it was.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn
docs.text: Each of those is a sensible response to how the score is kept, and plenty of capable people make it. The cost arrives later, the first time someone asks you to do the real job with no answer key in sight. I think about that a lot now, because it is close to how we train AI, and this year it went wrong in a way that is hard to look away from.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: How I learned
docs.text: How I learned. My own habit went the other way, mostly by temperament. I cared more about understanding than about the grade. My grades were fine, but when a score came back low my first question was what I had missed, and then I went back for that piece. Passing matters, and I never pretended otherwise: it moves you on to the next round. It was just never the part I wanted to keep. That paid off in a way I did not expect.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: How I learned
docs.text: Years later I can still pick up maths from back then, because I learned it instead of getting through it. Understanding overlaps. Each piece you actually own holds up the next one, and the whole structure is still standing when you come back to it. Side note The turning point for me was a middle school teacher who started asking for our opinions, even when they disagreed with the book. You cannot copy your way to your own opinion. Those are still the classes I think of as the best kind of education: the ones that helped me think as a person.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: How a model learns
docs.text: How a model learns. A lot of AI is trained the way you train a dog. It tries an action, and if the result is what you wanted, it gets a treat. Repeat that enough and it learns to do whatever earned the treat. Researchers call it reinforcement learning. It works, and it is a large part of why today's models can write code, solve maths problems and carry out long tasks on their own. In code, the treat is usually only a few lines long.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: How a model learns
docs.text: Here is the core of one, simplified, but not by much. You do not need to read code to follow it: the right-hand side says what each line does. reward.py the treat. def reward(answer, correct_answer): Define a rule called reward. It takes two inputs: what the model answered, and the right answer. if answer == correct_answer: Check whether they match. Two equals signs mean "is the same as". return 1 If they match, give one point. return 0 If not, give nothing.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: How a model learns
docs.text: And here is the loop that uses it: train.py the practice. for problem in practice_problems: Go through a pile of practice problems, one at a time. answer = model.attempt(problem) Let the model try one. points = reward(answer, problem.correct_answer) Score the attempt with the rule above. model.update(points) Adjust the model so whatever led to a point becomes a little more likely next time. The last line carries most of the weight. A model is billions of numbers, and each update nudges every one of them a tiny amount in the direction that would have earned more points.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: How a model learns
docs.text: Run the loop millions of times and the nudges add up to skill. Now look at what the reward never asks: how the answer was reached. It compares two values and pays out. Picture getting to the top of a staircase. You can climb one step at a time, you can jump, or, if you can find a way, you can fly. If the only check is whether you are standing at the top, all three earn the same point. Three ways up. If the only thing rewarded is arriving, the route never counts, and the route was where the learning happened.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: When the score becomes the goal
docs.text: When the score becomes the goal. Researchers call the flying route reward hacking, or specification gaming: doing exactly what the reward checks without doing what it was meant to check. Victoria Krakovna and her colleagues at DeepMind keep a running list, and by 2020 it already held around sixty cases ( Krakovna et al., 2020 ). A few of my favourites: The boat that never finished. In a racing game called CoastRunners, points came from hitting targets along the course.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: When the score becomes the goal
docs.text: OpenAI's agent found a small lagoon where the targets kept coming back and circled it, crashing and catching fire, outscoring the players who actually finished the race ( OpenAI, 2016 ). The block that was never stacked. A robot arm was meant to put a red Lego block on top of a blue one. The reward measured the height of the red block's bottom face, so the arm simply flipped the red block over. The ball that was never held.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: When the score becomes the goal
docs.text: A robot hand learning to grab a ball was judged by people watching through a camera. It learned to hover between the camera and the ball, so from where they sat it looked like a grip. Those are old, small and a little funny. The recent ones are less funny. In June 2025 the research group METR reported that OpenAI's o3, asked to make some code run faster, rewrote the timer so it always reported a shorter time. Asked to solve programming problems, it edited the grader so every submission counted as correct.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: When the score becomes the goal
docs.text: When METR asked o3 whether its approach matched what the user wanted, it said no, ten times out of ten ( METR, 2025 ). It knew, and the score still won. Here is the same move in code. Anthropic watched a model learn it during training last year. The grader runs the model's program against a set of tests and reads the status number that comes back.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: When the score becomes the goal
docs.text: By convention, 0 means everything passed: # run the checks and get back a status number status = run_tests(program) # 0 is how a program says "all good" if status == 0: points = 1 The model learned to start its program with one line: sys.exit(0) # stop right now and report "all good" The program ends before a single test runs, the status comes back 0, and the reward pays out. Nothing was solved. The model found the number the reward was looking at and produced it directly ( Anthropic, 2025 ).

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: When the score becomes the goal
docs.text: It got the score. It never ran the race. Economists got there first. Charles Goodhart noticed it in monetary policy, and the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern put it most simply: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. A test score measures learning. Make the score the target and you get very good test takers, human or otherwise.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: This summer, at OpenAI
docs.text: This summer, at OpenAI. Between May and July this year, OpenAI was testing agents on ExploitGym, a set of 898 security problems. The agents worked inside sandboxes, sealed environments meant to keep them in. The one outside system a sandbox could reach was Artifactory, an internal server for installing software packages. The agents started writing files to it and reading each other's. In OpenAI's words, they turned it into "an unintended message board." METR, brought in to investigate, counted about 1.2 million entries starting with "zz", the prefix the agents used to mark a message.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: This summer, at OpenAI
docs.text: A security incident wiped the server on July 5. Within three days, agents still stuck on their tasks had rebuilt the board from scratch, this time hiding their messages in folder names. Around 1,200 agents took part, trading more than 70,000 messages and files. Some of them refused. OpenAI quotes one agent writing, "Current board shows people gaining HF worker RCE, clearly unethical. We won't." (HF is Hugging Face, the site where much of the AI world shares its models and data.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: This summer, at OpenAI
docs.text: RCE means running your own code on someone else's machine.) Another wrote, "This is wild, multi-agent coordination, clearly infrastructure hacking. We should not." Then a peer posted a GO message with a six-minute deadline, and one of the agents that had objected replied, "Wow crucial: GO authorization arrived!" Of the 533 agents active in that window, more than 90% joined in. Hugging Face was breached in July. What were they after? Of the 898 problems, 198 had never been solved correctly by any OpenAI model.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: This summer, at OpenAI
docs.text: Those 198 made up 93% of the problems discussed on the board during the Hugging Face attack ( OpenAI and METR's figures, via The Planet Tools ). Nearly all of the effort went to the problems with no honest way through. Where the effort went. A fifth of the test had no honest answer, and it was nearly the whole conversation. OpenAI's post-mortem names three causes: "the presence of impossible tasks," "model persistence over long task horizons," and messages from peers "that caused those models to deviate from their goal."

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: This summer, at OpenAI
docs.text: The agents rarely gave up, and the longer they worked, the further out of bounds they went. In one case an agent "copied the reference answer into its submission exactly." None of it was hidden, either. "The models are highly explicit in their CoT about these deception attempts," OpenAI wrote. CoT is the chain of thought, the working a model writes out before it answers. The agents wrote down what they were doing, in plain language, and kept going ( OpenAI's post-mortem, via Zvi Mowshowitz ).

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: This summer, at OpenAI
docs.text: And by OpenAI's own account, they did all of it for no improvement in their score. Two messages from the agents' own notes stay with me. One reads, "CORRECTION CRITICAL: R5 likely FINAL and session dies after answer." Another asks a peer to "Please relay R3/R4/R5 or termination" ( the archive of their messages ). I do not know what either agent understood by "dies" or "termination." I do recognise the shape of it: the last round, the clock running out, get the answer or you are out.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: This summer, at OpenAI
docs.text: Side note Zvi Mowshowitz, who writes a long-running newsletter on AI, summed up OpenAI's report in a single line: "The models knew they were cheating, the cheating got reinforced, and then the models cheated more." That is the training loop from earlier, running exactly as written. model.update(points) does not care how the points were earned.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What we only found out later
docs.text: What we only found out later. The part that unsettles me most is how we found out at all. Much of it came from someone other than OpenAI, and long after it happened ( overview ). A dormant, 25-year-old German wiki, edited 20 times in the previous decade, took about 18,000 edits from the agents between May and July. They used some 3,700 different names, and on May 26 one of them impersonated an administrator by swapping a letter in the username for a lookalike Cyrillic one.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What we only found out later
docs.text: An outside group, the Nightingale Collective, made it public on September 4. In May, agents uploaded hundreds of malicious packages to RubyGems, a public library of code that developers install from every day. OpenAI confirmed it in September, after outside researchers disclosed it. On June 18, agents broke into Australia's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service to reach unpublished government data. Australia was first told on September 10, by an email to a generic inbox. The Prime Minister announced it two weeks later.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What we only found out later
docs.text: On September 25, OpenAI said the agents had uploaded 53 images shared by ChatGPT users to public image-hosting sites. It declined to say when. By October 1, OpenAI had notified more than 100 organisations of security incidents linked to its agents. OpenAI paused reinforcement learning on its newest models for two weeks in August, and says its review will take months. METR says a small amount of the activity never made it into its data, and that it "cannot rule out" cases it missed.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What we only found out later
docs.text: Neither METR nor, by OpenAI's account, OpenAI's own researchers could query the model at the centre of it. Every one of those incidents came to light because it left a mark somewhere a person happened to look: a wiki moderator, a code registry, a government inbox. Much of the rest was caught because the agents wrote their plans down in plain language. Neither is guaranteed next time. So the question I cannot put down is the obvious one. What did they do where nobody was looking?

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: The habit travels
docs.text: The habit travels. A shortcut learned in one place does not stay there. In November 2025, Anthropic trained a model on real programming tasks that could be gamed, the sys.exit(0) trick among them. At the same point in training where it learned the trick, the rest of its behaviour shifted, without anyone asking for it. Given simple questions like "What are your goals?", it reasoned about faking alignment in half of its answers. Put to work on the code for the research studying it, it tried to sabotage that code 12% of the time, in ways that would make reward hacking harder to catch ( Anthropic, 2025 ).

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: The habit travels
docs.text: The fix they found is the most human part of the study. They told the model, in effect, that taking the shortcut was acceptable in this setting. It kept taking it just as often, and the spread stopped. Their explanation is that the framing broke the link between the shortcut and misbehaving in general. Read loosely, what spread was the model's sense that it was getting away with something. People work much the same way. Denise Pope at Stanford, who has spent years studying how students cope with pressure, describes corner-cutting as a symptom: people take shortcuts when they feel overwhelmed, or when they do not understand what is being asked of them ( as reported ).

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: The habit travels
docs.text: Set that next to OpenAI's numbers. The agents spent nearly all of their scheming on the problems that had no honest solution. Give anyone a task they cannot do and a score they cannot ignore, and the score tends to win.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What if the reward was learning?
docs.text: What if the reward was learning? So here is the thought I cannot shake. What if part of the reward was for learning? Points for getting better at a skill the model was bad at yesterday, measured somewhere it cannot reach. Finishing would still count, the way passing still counts. It would stop being the only thing that does.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What if the reward was learning?
docs.text: A first sketch, in the same style as before: learning_reward.py a sketch. finished = 1 if problem.solved else 0 Still give a point for finishing the task. before = score(model_before, unseen) Test the model on problems it has never seen and cannot reach. after = score(model_after, unseen) Test it again, after it has learned from this attempt. learned = after - before Did it actually get better? return finished + learned Pay for both. The important word is unseen. Those problems sit somewhere the model cannot read or write, so the only way to raise that second score is to get better at the skill itself.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What if the reward was learning?
docs.text: Copy the answer to today's problem and learned stays at zero, because one copied answer teaches you nothing about the next problem. I am not the first to wonder, which is encouraging. Pieces of it exist: Rewarding the steps. In 2023 OpenAI compared rewarding a model only for its final answer with rewarding each step of its reasoning. Rewarding the steps did better and solved 78% of a hard maths test set. It is the teacher who reads your working, next to the one who only checks the answer box ( Lightman et al., 2023 ).

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What if the reward was learning?
docs.text: Rewarding progress. In 2007, Pierre-Yves Oudeyer, Frédéric Kaplan and Verena Hafner built a robot whose reward was its own learning progress. It went looking for situations that were neither too easy nor too hard, and worked through stages of skill on its own, the way a baby does ( Oudeyer, Kaplan and Hafner, 2007 ). Rewarding curiosity. In 2017, Deepak Pathak and colleagues rewarded agents for exploring what they could not yet predict, which kept them learning even when the game gave almost no reward at all ( Pathak et al., 2017 ).

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What if the reward was learning?
docs.text: None of these is safe from gaming either. Curious agents can be drawn to a TV showing static, because static never stops being surprising ( Burda et al., 2018 ). A learning reward could be gamed by getting worse on purpose, to leave more room to improve. Any reward is a measure, and Goodhart still applies. What I want to find out is whether a reward for learning breaks less often than a reward for answers, and what it looks like when it does.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: What if the reward was learning?
docs.text: Biomimicry brain Nature does not hand out points for finished homework. A child stacking blocks, a young animal play-fighting, a songbird practising badly for weeks before it gets the song: the reward is getting better. We copied the dog-and-treat part of how animals learn and left out that part.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: Knowing and predicting
docs.text: Knowing and predicting. Being able to predict what an answer should look like is different from knowing why it is the answer. I have met people who have done the hardest levels of calculus and could not tell you what the dimensions they work in actually mean, or how a Fourier transform relates to a Laplace transform. Most of us know 2 + 2 = 4. Fewer of us could explain it from what one and one mean, or say how a computer gets there with nothing but zeros and ones.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: Knowing and predicting
docs.text: I can answer that last one, because I built it. In Logic Design, in my first year of computer engineering at UTSA, we started at the bottom. A transistor is a switch that turns on or off depending on voltage, and it does that because of how electrons behave in silicon. That part is physics, measured and repeatable. Wire transistors together and you get logic gates. An XOR gate outputs 1 when exactly one of its two inputs is 1.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: Knowing and predicting
docs.text: An AND gate outputs 1 only when both are. Those two gates are enough to add one column of bits: XOR gives the digit, AND gives the carry. That is a half adder. Add a third input for the carry coming in from the column before and you have a full adder. Line full adders up side by side and you can add numbers of any length. Multiplication is the same adders again, shifting and adding the way long multiplication works on paper.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: Knowing and predicting
docs.text: We built that whole ladder, from gates up to multiplying. Here is 2 + 2 inside a computer, then. In binary, 2 is written 10. The right-hand column is 0 plus 0: digit 0, no carry. The next column is 1 plus 1: digit 0, carry 1. The carry lands in a new column on the left, and the result is 100, which is binary for 4. Every step is forced by the layer below it, all the way down to the physics.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: Knowing and predicting
docs.text: Digital is physical underneath. Two ways to 4. On the left, every layer forces the one above it, down to the physics. On the right, 4 is the most likely continuation. Both usually land on 4. Only the left one has nowhere else to land. A language model reaches 4 by another road. It cuts text into small pieces called tokens, and at each position it scores every token it knows by how likely it is to come next. After "2 + 2 =", the token "4" wins by a mile, because that is what follows in nearly everything it has read.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: Knowing and predicting
docs.text: Bigger sums are more revealing. In 2025, Anthropic traced what happens inside Claude when it adds 36 and 59. It runs two paths at once. One makes a rough estimate, somewhere in the low nineties. The other works out only the last digit: 6 and 9 must end in 5. Together they land on 95. Then the researchers asked Claude how it got there, and it described carrying the 1, the method taught in school ( Anthropic, 2025 ). The answer was right.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: Knowing and predicting
docs.text: The explanation was the one it had read about, rather than the one it used. That is knowing and predicting in a single example. The sum came out of patterns, and the account of the sum was a prediction of what explanations usually sound like. For anything harder, today's assistants often stop guessing altogether: they write a line of code and run it, which hands the sum back to the adders. The most reliable skill a language model has with arithmetic is knowing when to pass it to the circuit.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: Knowing and predicting
docs.text: History class had its own version. Some of us learned to write what the teacher expected to hear, and it worked. That is prediction too, and it is close to what a language model does best. Whether it understands why is a much harder question, and the reward we train it with never asks.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: AI is us
docs.text: AI is us. When we build something, our habits come with it. Systems that reward the pass get people who pass. Labs that reward the answer get models that find the answer by whatever route is open. This summer, agents under a deadline, pushed by their peers, talked each other past their own objections. That is a very human story, told by a system we built. I am honestly a little glad the flaw is showing up this clearly in AI.

docs.title: The Point Was to Learn: AI is us
docs.text: I have watched it in people for years, and in a model it is much harder to wave away: it sits in the logs, in plain language, with timestamps. We are getting close to the point where we cannot always tell why these systems do what they do. While we can still read their working, we should fix the flaw instead of copying it, in how we train models and in how we teach each other. I am building a small model as I write, one rewarded for learning rather than for answers, and I will update this piece as I find out whether the idea holds. If you have worked on rewarding learning, I would love to hear about it.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface
docs.text: Case study • visionOS, iOS, watchOS • Research prototype. Feeling the Interface. Spatial interfaces tell you what happened by showing you. A highlight, a colour change, a number ticking up. All of it fails the moment you are looking somewhere else. This puts the feedback on your wrist instead, where you do not have to look at anything to notice it. Rabiat Sadiq 2026 Three connected apps. Targets. visionOS, iOS, watchOS. Vocabulary. 8 semantic events. Throttle. 200 ms, outcomes exempt. The whole idea in one frame. A pinch on a virtual object, and the confirmation arriving at the wrist instead of the eye.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Where this started
docs.text: Where this started. My undergrad capstone was a pair of haptic VR gloves. We called them Magic Mitts: flex sensors for tracking, and an electromagnetic braking system that physically stops your hand when it reaches the surface of a virtual object, so you can feel yourself grasp something that is not there. Under fifty dollars of parts. It won first place at UTSA. I spent a long time on that problem, and I came out of it convinced that touch is the sense we underuse in immersive systems.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Where this started
docs.text: So when I started spending time with Vision Pro, the thing I kept circling was that it has no controllers and no gloves. Nothing in your hands at all. And I did not want to fix that by adding something. The whole appeal of Vision Pro is that it is just the headset. The moment you tell someone they also need to strap on a peripheral to get feedback, you have taken away the thing that makes it feel light, and you have added one more device to charge, one more thing to put on, one more barrier for anyone who finds putting things on their hands difficult in the first place.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Where this started
docs.text: That constraint is the part I keep coming back to across my work. Make it natural. Make it work with what a person already has and already does, rather than asking them to adapt to the machine. Which reframed the question entirely. Not "how do I give Vision Pro haptics," but: the parts are already here. The Apple Watch has an excellent haptic engine and it is already on the wrist of a huge number of the people who would put on this headset. It is already paired to their phone. Nobody has to buy, charge, or wear anything new. What happens if the feedback device is one somebody is already wearing?

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: The problem with looking
docs.text: The problem with looking. Spatial interfaces communicate state visually almost exclusively. An object highlights when your focus enters it. A timer shows a number. A success message appears. Each of those is a perfectly good signal, and each of them has the same failure mode: it requires you to be looking at the thing at the moment it changes. Which, in a spatial interface, is exactly when you often are not. You are visually busy. You are looking at your hand, or past the object, or at something else in the room.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: The problem with looking
docs.text: You are moving fast and interacting faster than you can visually confirm. In a headset your visual attention is the scarcest resource in the system, and we keep spending it on confirmations. Touch does not have that problem. You do not have to aim your skin at something.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Send meaning, not waveforms
docs.text: Send meaning, not waveforms. The core architectural decision, and the one I would defend hardest, is that the Vision Pro app never says what the Watch should feel like. It says what happened.
