There are eight semantic events in the vocabulary: a focus entering an interactive object, a timer incrementing, a timer crossing a major threshold, a timer starting, a timer finishing, a grab succeeding, a drop failing, and a basket being scored. The visionOS layer emits one of those.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Send meaning, not waveforms
docs.text: The Watch owns the entire question of how each one should feel. That split matters more than it looks. It means the haptic vocabulary can be retuned, or completely rewritten, without touching the spatial app at all. It means the same event can feel different on different hardware. And during a study, it means I can change what a success feels like between participants without changing a line of interaction code, which is the whole point of building it as a research prototype rather than a demo.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Send meaning, not waveforms
docs.text: The debug panel, running in the visionOS simulator. Every event in the vocabulary is fireable by hand, with a live event log and running counts of what was sent versus what got rate limited. This screen exists so that during a session I can trigger any event on demand without having to reproduce the interaction that normally causes it. The chain. Three apps, in a line. visionOS detects the interaction and produces a semantic event. An iPhone sits in the middle as a relay, because the headset does not talk to the Watch directly, and passes the event along over WatchConnectivity.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Send meaning, not waveforms
docs.text: The Watch receives it, applies its rate limits, and plays a system haptic. Figure 1. The payload is deliberately tiny: an event name, the scenario it came from, and a timestamp. Small enough that the link is never the bottleneck.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: The rate limiting is the design
docs.text: The rate limiting is the design. Apple already solved the hard part here, and it is worth being clear about that. The Watch has an excellent haptic engine, and more importantly its vocabulary is already legible to people. We all already understand a small tap for every increment of a value, the way a timer picker on your phone clicks as you spin it past each minute. Nobody needs that explained. What breaks is quantity. A spatial interface can fire a focus-entered event dozens of times a second while your hand drifts across a boundary, and if every one of those becomes a tap, the Watch turns into a wasp.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: The rate limiting is the design
docs.text: Good taps, far too many of them. So there is a shared throttle, and the important part is that it is not uniform. Events are split into two classes. Click-class events get throttled. Focus entering a target and timer increments are repeatable by nature. Clicks are limited to one every 200 ms, and re-entering a target has its own 300 ms cooldown on top of that. Outcome events always pass. A grab succeeding, a drop failing, a threshold being crossed, a timer finishing, a basket scoring.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: The rate limiting is the design
docs.text: These are things that happened once and matter. They bypass the throttle entirely. That distinction is the actual product thinking in this project. A confirmation you can miss is only annoying. An outcome you miss is a bug. So the system is allowed to drop the former and never the latter. The limiter is shared code that runs in two places: on the Watch, where it is authoritative, and on visionOS, where it exists purely to avoid flooding the link with events that are going to be discarded anyway.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Three scenarios to feel
docs.text: Three scenarios to feel. Alongside the debug panel above, which is a harness rather than an experience, there are three built scenarios. Each produces a genuinely different kind of event, so the vocabulary gets exercised rather than just demonstrated. Timer: continuous adjustment against meaningful landmarks. Every increment is a small throttled tap, but crossing 5, 10, 15, 30 or 60 minutes sends a distinct one. This is the scenario that tests whether you can set a value without looking at the number, which is something you genuinely cannot do with a purely visual control.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Three scenarios to feel
docs.text: Objects: encounter, grab, and failure. Entering the cube's active region fires one tap. Actually moving it past a small distance threshold counts as a real grab rather than a twitch, and confirms. Dropping it outside the zone fails, and failure gets its own feel. Three different states in one gesture, none of which you have to look at. Basketball: the pure outcome. One event, one moment, no ambiguity. This is the control case. If a scored basket does not feel unmistakable on the wrist, the whole premise is in trouble.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: The part I keep thinking about
docs.text: The part I keep thinking about. Building this made me notice something about feedback generally, and it lands on biomimicry, which is where a lot of my thinking ends up. Anyone who has worked with me knows I will get there eventually. Proprioception, the sense that tells you where your own hand is without looking at it, is doing constant, silent, unglamorous confirmation work. You do not notice it until it is gone. Nobody has ever thought "what a satisfying proprioceptive response" while picking up a cup.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: The part I keep thinking about
docs.text: The feedback is good precisely because it does not ask for attention. That is a hard standard for an interface, because every incentive pushes the other way. A haptic that announces itself demos well. A haptic that quietly keeps you oriented does not demo at all. But the second one is what a body actually does, and I think it is the right target. Which is also why the Watch decides how things feel rather than the headset. In a body, the limb reports its own state. It does not wait for the brain to specify a waveform.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Status and what I would test
docs.text: Status and what I would test. This is a working research prototype, not a shipping app, and it was scoped that way on purpose. It is not a production timer, it does not do continuous frame-by-frame vibration from hand tracking, it does not build custom haptic waveforms, and it does not do multi-user anything. What I want to find out with it: Which spatial events actually benefit from tactile confirmation, and which ones are just noise on the wrist. My guess is that outcomes benefit far more than encounters, but that is a guess and the prototype exists to check it.

docs.title: Feeling the Interface: Status and what I would test
docs.text: Whether the 200 ms throttle is anywhere near right. It is a starting number, not a finding. It may well be too aggressive for slow deliberate interactions and too permissive for fast ones, in which case it should adapt to interaction speed rather than being fixed. Whether people can distinguish the semantic events from each other at all without being told, or whether the vocabulary needs to be much smaller than eight. Whether the wrist is even the right place. It is the convenient place, because that is where the hardware already is, and convenient and correct are not the same thing. All projects GitHub.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets
docs.text: Essay • watchOS Swipe Surface • Why I started it. Hands in Your Pockets. The Apple Watch is sold as a health tracker that happens to have a screen. Take the strap off and look at what is left: a small bright puck with a haptic engine and a radio to every other device you own. This is about the day I stopped seeing it as a watch. Rabiat Sadiq September 18, 2026 About an 8 minute read. Picture someone standing somewhere.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets
docs.text: Their phone is propped in front of them, or an iPad, or they have a headset on. How do they interact with it without it looking like anything? That was the first question, and it is older than this project. I had it back when I was thinking about hardware: some little hard square of a device, something you could hold in a pocket with a hand that looks like it is just resting there. Small gestures, nothing that reads as tapping the air or touching everything in the room.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets
docs.text: Not obvious that you have glasses on. Not obvious that you are doing anything at all. I imagined building that device myself. Then I switched to building for iOS, looked at the Watch properly for the first time, and realised the thing I wanted to make was already on my wrist. Side note The reason I was suddenly building iOS at all: I got a new MacBook. I love my PC, I love that it runs Unity and everything I need for VR, and I will keep going back to it.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets
docs.text: But having Xcode and an M5 chip, and moving with AI alongside me the way I learned to at CMU, means an idea can be a running app before I have finished deciding whether it is worth pursuing. I build to find out. Some nights I do not sleep because there is too much I could make. This project came out of one of those nights.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: Use what people already carry
docs.text: Use what people already carry. There is a version of this idea that involves designing a new object. I did not want that one. I come from somewhere where resources were finite and you made things with what you had, and that instinct has never left. It is why the Vision Pro haptics project used a Watch that was already on the wrist instead of a new peripheral, and it is why this one does too. Apple's ecosystem is the other half of the argument.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: Use what people already carry
docs.text: Whatever else you think about the company, the devices talk to each other well. So instead of a new thing, the question becomes: what can the existing things do together that none of them was sold for? I had just got a new Watch. I remember seeing it without the straps, and it was exactly the puck I had been imagining. Bright screen, a haptic engine, a radio link. Everything the hypothetical device needed, already manufactured, already paired. Hands in your pockets, a flick of the thumb, and the screen across the room does the thing.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: Subtle is the point
docs.text: Subtle is the point. Voice is having a moment. Hey Siri, audio assistants, the whole rise of talking to your devices. That is genuinely great, and there are a lot of situations where I do not want to talk to anything. On a train. In a meeting. Standing in a kitchen with a recipe propped up and my hands covered in something. Next to a sleeping person. Your eyes are already on the screen. You already know exactly what you want it to do. The gap is only in how you tell it. A flick in your pocket closes that gap without a sound, without a raised hand, without anyone else in the room being able to tell it happened.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: A watch is also a thing
docs.text: A watch is also a thing. This is the part I found most interesting, and it is a little embarrassing that it took me this long. To build it I had to take my eyes off the Watch as a watch. Yes, it tells the time. Yes, it counts steps. But it is also just a device. A thing. A very small touch surface that happens to be worn. It is like the ice cream bowl you use for everything except ice cream.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: A watch is also a thing
docs.text: Nobody designed it for cereal, keys, or the hair ties by the sink. It works anyway, because a bowl is a bowl before it is an ice cream bowl. Side note A while ago I saw the Boston Dynamics robots moving in ways no human moves. Walking backwards at speed, folding, rolling. There is a version of robotics that only wants to recreate how we walk, and I understand it, but why would a machine be limited to us? Why not go past what our bodies happen to do? I keep thinking about that when I look at a Watch and only see a watch. The object is allowed to go past what it was made for.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: What Apple left on the table
docs.text: What Apple left on the table. Before building I went looking for who had done this. Apple ships almost exactly this gesture grammar already: the Watch can be a remote for Apple TV, it can drive Keynote, and the keyboard on the phone has had swipe for years. Watch gestures reach the iPhone in one more place, inside the VoiceOver accessibility path. And that is the whole list. There is no general purpose Watch swipe surface for the phone, and there is no public API that would let a third party build one outside of its own app.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: What Apple left on the table
docs.text: I do not know why. Maybe the devices are meant to stay separate as a matter of principle. Maybe it is coming and I will feel silly. I looked, I did not find much, so I am building it. That constraint shapes what this can be right now. A third party app cannot control the system interface, so what I can build is a prototype of what it would feel like, inside an app that owns its own content. Which is fine.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: What Apple left on the table
docs.text: A prototype that is honest about being one is how you find out whether the idea deserves the rest. Side note The other constraint is dumber: I am close to the limit on how many apps one developer account can have installed at a time. This is not a limit designed for someone who wants to pop out a project every other day.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: What it is so far
docs.text: What it is so far. The phone app has four modes, and each one decides what the five gestures mean while it is showing. The Watch pad labels its own edges with the current mode's meanings, so a flick always says what it will do before you make it. The four pads. Reader for recipes, scores and manuals propped up while your hands are busy. Photos for a set across the table. Slides for a deck on the phone or a mirrored display.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: What it is so far
docs.text: Prompter for a script rolling past a reading line. Same five gestures, different meanings, always labelled. On the Watch, the whole screen is the pad. Drags are classified by their dominant axis, diagonals and brushes are ignored, and a short fast flick counts on its predicted travel. Each direction has its own haptic. The Digital Crown scrolls the reader, steps slides, scrubs video and nudges the prompter. On newer Watches the pinch gesture, Double Tap, triggers select, so a flick and a select never need the other hand.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: What it is so far
docs.text: Flicks made while the phone is out of reach are queued and delivered on the next connection. Every flick is logged on the phone with its direction, speed and one way latency, so the link itself can be measured rather than trusted. I want to know what the delay feels like before I have opinions about it. Reader on the phone. The hands doing the cooking never touch it. Prompter. Faster and slower are a thumb in a pocket.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: Is this one thread?
docs.text: Is this one thread? People will notice the sequence. Haptic gloves in undergrad. Wrist haptics for Vision Pro. Now the wrist as the input. I do not honestly experience those as one deliberate thread. What I do see is a connection in what I keep reaching for: haptics, the interactions that are already available on a body, lightweight wearables, things that make life easier without announcing themselves. Some of this is just where my head is. I have just finished a masters in human computer interaction, and interfaces and interactions are the top of my mind whether I want them there or not.

docs.title: Hands in Your Pockets: Is this one thread?
docs.text: There is no machine learning in this project. It is still an idea worth chasing, and I have stopped needing every idea to have a model in it. The roadmap after the phone is Apple TV, then Vision Pro. Since the Watch to phone link is iOS and watchOS only, whether those need the phone as a bridge or a direct path is itself one of the questions, and I would rather find out by building it than by reading about it. I cannot wait to test it standing up, hands in my pockets, with something on the other side of the room. Field Notes GitHub.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text: Lab. New models come out every day. This is where I try them before building them into anything: what they can and can't do, and how they run on your own device. Nothing to install, nothing uploaded. By the month each model came out, newest first. The ones that run here say how big they are and where they will run before anything downloads, and stay on your device after the first visit. The ones too big for a browser link to a demo instead.

docs.title: Depth Anything V2
docs.text: Depth Anything V2, by HKU and TikTok. Lab model: Space, Depth. Give it any photo and it works out how far away every pixel is, so the photo tilts like a small 3D scene. Try it on your phone and move it around. Drop in a photo and tilt it in 3D. 24.8M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: Moonshine
docs.text: Moonshine, by Moonshine AI. Lab model: Audio, Speech to text. Speech to text made small enough for a phone. Talk and your words show up as you say them. Your voice never leaves your device. Talk, and your words appear as you say them. 27M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: MIT.

docs.title: gpt-oss-20b
docs.text: gpt-oss-20b, by OpenAI. Lab model: Language, Reasoning chat. OpenAI's first open-weight language model since GPT-2. It reasons step by step, uses tools, and runs on a laptop with 16 GB of memory, just not inside a browser tab. Too big to run here: 21 billion parameters, about 13 GB. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: Qwen-Image-Edit
docs.text: Qwen-Image-Edit, by Alibaba Qwen. Lab model: Vision, Image editing. Edit a photo by describing the change: swap the background, fix the words on a sign, turn a character to face the other way. Too big to run here: 20 billion parameters, tens of gigabytes. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: TRELLIS.2
docs.text: TRELLIS.2, by Microsoft. Lab model: Space, Image to 3D. One picture in, a textured 3D model out, ready for a game engine or a VR scene. The weights are MIT; the full pipeline also loads two helper models with their own licences. Too big to run here: 4 billion parameters plus helper models, many gigabytes. Licence: MIT.

docs.title: FLUX.2 [klein] 4B
docs.text: FLUX.2 [klein] 4B, by Black Forest Labs. Lab model: Vision, Image generation. A small, fast image generator and editor from the makers of FLUX. Only the 4B size is Apache licensed; the larger one is not. Too big to run here: 4 billion parameters, about 8 GB. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: ACE-Step 1.5
docs.text: ACE-Step 1.5, by ACE Studio and StepFun. Lab model: Audio, Music generation. Write a prompt and lyrics, get a full song with vocals in seconds on a good GPU. Too big to run here: several gigabytes of weights. Licence: MIT.

docs.title: Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime
docs.text: Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime, by Mistral AI. Lab model: Audio, Live transcription. Speech to text that keeps up as you talk, in many languages. A WebGPU version exists, but it is a multi-gigabyte download, so here it is a demo instead. Too big to run here: 4.4 billion parameters, several gigabytes. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: EdgeTAM
docs.text: EdgeTAM, by Meta. Lab model: Vision, Cut-outs. Meta's on-device take on Segment Anything 2. Tap anything in a photo and it lifts out as a clean cut-out, ready to drop into a game or a VR scene. Tap anything in a photo to lift it out. 10M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: TeleOCR
docs.text: TeleOCR, by XingChen-AGI. Lab model: Vision, Document reading. A small vision language model that reads documents: printed pages, receipts, handwriting, tables and formulas. Point it at a photo and it writes out what it sees. Drop in a photo of a page and watch it read. 1.4B parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: Strands Decider 2B
docs.text: Strands Decider 2B, by Strands Labs. Lab model: Language, Decisions. A decision model: it does not write, it picks. Give it a situation and some options and it gives each one a calibrated probability in a single pass. Describe a dilemma, list your options, and see how it leans. 2B parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: mdbr-leaf-ir
docs.text: mdbr-leaf-ir, by MongoDB. Lab model: Language, Search. A tiny search model that matches by meaning, not by keywords. Here it searches everything I have built and written, right in your browser. Search my work by what you mean. 23M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: RF-DETR Nano
docs.text: RF-DETR Nano, by Roboflow. Lab model: Vision, Object detection. Point a camera and it boxes and names what it sees, many times a second. A detection transformer small enough for a phone, with no clean-up pass for overlapping boxes. Point your camera and watch it name things live. 30.5M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: DPDFNet
docs.text: DPDFNet, by Ceva. Lab model: Audio, Noise removal. Takes the noise out of speech: cafe chatter, fans, rain. It is small and streaming, built for earbuds and calls, and here it cleans a whole clip several times faster than it takes to play. Bury a voice in noise, then clean it back out. 2.6M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: Chronos-2
docs.text: Chronos-2, by Amazon. Lab model: Data, Forecasting. Give it any series of numbers, steps, sales, power use, and it says what probably comes next, with a band for how sure it is. It has never seen your data and needs no training on it. Pick a series and watch the forecast fan out. 120M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: Soprano
docs.text: Soprano, by Eugene Kwek. Lab model: Audio, Text to speech. Type a sentence and hear it read aloud, in a clear and natural voice. It is small enough to run in a browser tab and starts talking before it has finished the sentence. Type a sentence, hear it spoken. 80M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: Teach it by example
docs.text: Teach it by example, by Google. Lab model: Vision, Teach by example. Google's Teachable Machine idea from 2017, rebuilt on a modern image model: show it a few examples of two things, and it tells them apart live. Nothing is trained on a server; it all happens in your browser. Teach it two things with a few photos, then watch it guess. 93M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: AudioSeal
docs.text: AudioSeal, by Meta. Lab model: Audio, Watermarking. Hides a short ID inside speech where you can't hear it, then finds it again, down to which parts of a clip carry it. Noise, cuts and volume barely touch it; a small change of speed wipes it out. Stamp a voice with a hidden ID, then try to scrub it off. 23M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: MIT.

docs.title: AIFS 2.0
docs.text: AIFS 2.0, by ECMWF. Lab model: Science, Weather forecasting. The machine-learning weather model from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, released with open weights. Too big to run here: about 1 GB of weights and global weather data as input. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Boltz-2
docs.text: Boltz-2, by MIT Jameel Clinic and Recursion. Lab model: Science, Protein structure. Predicts the 3D shape of proteins and how strongly a drug-like molecule binds to them, an open alternative to AlphaFold 3 for that job. Too big to run here: hundreds of millions of parameters and a big GPU. Licence: MIT.

docs.title: Evo 2
docs.text: Evo 2, by Arc Institute. Lab model: Science, DNA. A language model for DNA across all of life. It can predict which mutations break a gene and even write new genetic sequences. Too big to run here: 1 to 40 billion parameters. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: FourCastNet 3
docs.text: FourCastNet 3, by NVIDIA. Lab model: Science, Weather forecasting. A neural weather model that forecasts the whole planet days to weeks ahead in minutes on a single GPU, a job that takes physics models a supercomputer. Too big to run here: gigabytes of weights and global weather data as input. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: Matrix-Game 3.0
docs.text: Matrix-Game 3.0, by Skywork. Lab model: Space, World model. A world model: instead of a game engine, a neural network imagines the next frame of a 3D world as you move through it with the keyboard and mouse. Too big to run here: more than 5 billion parameters and a large GPU. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: SmolVLA
docs.text: SmolVLA, by Hugging Face. Lab model: Space, Robot brain. A small vision-language-action model: it looks through a robot's cameras, reads an instruction like "put the cube in the box", and outputs the arm's next moves. Trained on community robot data and small enough for a gaming laptop. Too big to run here: 450 million parameters, and it needs a robot or a simulator to drive. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: X-VLA
docs.text: X-VLA, by Tsinghua AIR. Lab model: Space, Robot brain. One model that drives many different robots, from single arms to two-armed setups, by learning a small "prompt" per robot body. Too big to run here: about 0.9 billion parameters plus a robot to drive. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: ZUNA1.1
docs.text: ZUNA1.1, by Zyphra. Lab model: Body, Brain signals. A foundation model for EEG, the electrical signals of the brain. It can rebuild a missing electrode from the others and turn messy recordings into something models can learn from. Too big to run here: 380 million parameters, about 1.5 GB. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: G1 Walking Policy
docs.text: G1 Walking Policy, by Julien Blanchon and mjswan. Lab model: Space, Robot walking. A humanoid robot that taught itself to walk in simulation, running live in your browser. Shove it and watch a small network catch its balance, fifty times a second. Shove a walking robot and watch it catch itself. 219K parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: Apache 2.0.

docs.title: ME-rPPG
docs.text: ME-rPPG, by Tsinghua University. Lab model: Body, Heart rate. Your pulse, from your webcam. Each heartbeat shifts the colour of your skin very slightly, and this tiny model turns those shifts into a pulse wave and a heart rate. The video never leaves your device. Look at the camera for ten seconds. 0.58M parameters. Runs on your own device in the browser, nothing uploaded. Licence: MIT.

docs.title: Demo Check
docs.text: Demo Check. Language · Demo reliability. Claude API · bring your own key. Run a Claude demo 5 to 20 times before you show it once: pass rate, latency, every failure checked by code, and a recorded passing run to fall back on.

docs.title: Study Lab
docs.text: Study Lab. Science · Study tools. ML · Audio · Circuits · VR · Design · Physics · Biology · Muscles · Elements. Nine hands on subjects: machine learning from regression to LLMs and agents, sound and audio, live circuits, how VR works, UI design and UX laws, physics simulations, biology for pre-med, muscles on a 3D body and the periodic table. Runs in your browser.

docs.title: Study Lab
docs.text: Study Lab, part of the Lab. What do you want to learn? Hands on study labs, each built around one subject. Every chapter has a live demo, a plain words explanation, a going deeper part and a short check. Everything runs on your device and your scores stay in this browser. Subjects: Machine learning, Audio, Circuits, VR and XR, Design, Physics, Biology, Muscles, Elements.

docs.title: Study Lab: Machine learning
docs.text: Machine learning, a Study Lab subject. From fitting a line to neural networks, convolutions, how LLMs write and how agents use tools. 27 hands on chapters.

docs.title: ML Lab: what it covers
docs.text: ML Lab. Machine learning from the first idea to how chatbots and agents work, one hands on demo at a time. Machine learning is teaching a computer by example instead of by rules. Each chapter here is one idea you can poke at: drag points, train a tiny network, slide a filter across an image, watch a model pick its next word. Start at the top if ML is new to you, or jump to what you are curious about.

docs.title: ML Lab: chapters
docs.text: ML Lab chapters. What is machine learning: Rules versus examples. Data, features, labels and a model. Fitting a line: Linear regression and the loss you are trying to shrink. Gradient descent: How a model learns: roll downhill on the loss. Drawing a boundary: Logistic regression and probabilities. Nearest neighbours: Vote with the k closest examples. Decision trees: Twenty questions, learned from data. Overfitting: Memorising versus learning, train versus test. Is it any good?: Accuracy, precision, recall and the confusion matrix.

docs.title: ML Lab: chapters
docs.text: K-means clustering: Find groups nobody labelled. Squashing dimensions: PCA: keep the directions that matter most. Learning by reward: An agent learns a maze from trial and error. A single neuron: Weights, bias and an activation. Neural network playground: Stack neurons, train live, watch the boundary bend. Backpropagation: How blame flows backwards through a network. Images are numbers: Pixels, channels and grids of values. Convolution: Slide a small filter over an image and find edges. Inside a CNN: Layers of feature maps, in 3D, from edges to objects.

docs.title: ML Lab: chapters
docs.text: Tokens: How text becomes pieces a model can read. Embeddings: Meaning as a place in space. Attention: Each word looks at the others to understand itself. The transformer: One block at a time, the architecture behind LLMs. How an LLM writes: Next word odds, temperature and sampling. How LLMs are trained: Pretraining, fine tuning and feedback. Retrieval (RAG): Look things up before answering. Agents: A model in a loop with tools. Step through one. Multimodal models: Images, audio and text in one shared space. Diffusion: Make images by removing noise, step by step.

docs.title: Study Lab: Audio
docs.text: Audio, a Study Lab subject. Sound from air pressure to bits: frequency, harmonics, the spectrum, sampling, filters, EQ and compression.

docs.title: Audio Lab: what it covers
docs.text: Audio Lab. Sound and digital audio from air pressure to bits, one hands on demo at a time. Sound is air pushing on your ears. Digital audio is a long list of numbers that describes that push. Each chapter here is one idea you can hear and see: slide a pitch up past your hearing, build a square wave out of sines, watch your voice as a spectrogram, make a tone fold back above Nyquist, crush the bits, EQ a little band and feel latency in your own fingers. Start at the top if this is new, or jump to what you are curious about. Headphones help, and start with the volume low.

docs.title: Audio Lab: chapters
docs.text: Audio Lab chapters. What sound is: Air pressure waves, compressions and a speaker cone. Frequency and pitch: Hertz, notes, the range of hearing and your own limit. Amplitude and loudness: Decibels, the log scale and safe listening. Waveforms and timbre: Harmonics, and building a square wave out of sines. The spectrum: FFT, time versus frequency, and a live spectrogram. Sampling and sample rate: Samples, Nyquist and aliasing you can hear. Bit depth and quantisation: Steps, quantisation noise, dither and dynamic range.

docs.title: Audio Lab: chapters
docs.text: Bandwidth and filters: Low pass, high pass, band pass, notch and the telephone. EQ and mixing: A live band to balance with faders, pan and a 5 band EQ. Compression and file formats: Bitrate, lossless and lossy, masking, and file sizes. Stereo, phase and space: Panning, cancellation, echo, reverb and binaural cues. In and out: Microphone to speaker, and the latency in between.

docs.title: Study Lab: Circuits
docs.text: Circuits, a Study Lab subject. Build circuits and watch current flow. Ohm's law, series and parallel, capacitors, LEDs and fuses.

docs.title: Circuits Lab: what it covers
docs.text: Circuits Lab. Electricity from the first spark of an idea to building your own circuits, in a live simulator. Every chapter here runs the same real circuit simulator. The little moving dots are the current: they speed up when more current flows and stop when the path is broken. Drag parts in, draw wires, flip switches and watch what happens. Start at the top if electricity is new to you, or jump straight to the sandbox.

docs.title: Circuits Lab: chapters
docs.text: Circuits Lab chapters. What electricity is: Charge, current and voltage, next to a water circuit. Series circuits: One path: bulbs share the voltage and dim. Parallel circuits: Many paths: every bulb gets the full voltage. Power and energy: P = V I, brightness, and what a kWh costs. Short circuits and fuses: Why a short is dangerous and how a fuse saves you. Switches and logic: AND, OR, and the two way staircase switch. Capacitors: Charging and discharging, and the time constant RC. LEDs and diodes: One way current, forward voltage, and the resistor you need. Sandbox: Free build with presets, save and load.

docs.title: Study Lab: VR and XR
docs.text: VR and XR, a Study Lab subject. How headsets trick your eyes: stereo depth, lenses, tracking, latency, foveated rendering and comfort.

docs.title: VR Lab: what it covers
docs.text: VR Lab. How virtual and mixed reality actually work, from your two eyes to the WebXR API. A headset is a pair of tiny screens, two lenses, a set of sensors and a computer racing a deadline. Each chapter here takes one piece apart with a live 3D demo: see depth with red and cyan glasses, warp a grid the way a lens does, feel latency make the world swim, then fix it with reprojection. Start at the top if XR is new to you, or jump to what you are curious about.

docs.title: VR Lab: chapters
docs.text: VR Lab chapters. VR, AR, MR and XR: The reality to virtuality continuum, as a slider. Two eyes, depth: Stereo rendering, IPD, disparity and an anaglyph you can view with red and cyan glasses. Lenses and the headset: Magnifier optics, virtual image distance, distortion pre-warp and colour fringes. Field of view: Your visual field versus a headset, and what a narrow window feels like. Tracking: 3DoF and 6DoF: Rotation versus position, inside-out cameras, IMU drift and SLAM. Motion to photon: Make the world swim with latency, then fix it with prediction and timewarp.

docs.title: VR Lab: chapters
docs.text: The rendering pipeline: Two eyes, a frame budget, pixels per degree and foveated rendering. Vergence and focus: Why your eyes disagree with themselves in a headset. Motion sickness and comfort: Vection, vignettes, snap turns and teleporting. Interaction: Rays, gaze and pinch, direct touch and Fitts's law in 3D. Passthrough and mixed reality: Camera passthrough, occlusion, planes and anchors. Build for VR on the web: WebXR in a few lines, and a live Enter VR button.

docs.title: Study Lab: Design
docs.text: Design, a Study Lab subject. UI styles from skeuomorphism to glass, plus white space, hierarchy, colour, type and the UX laws you can measure.

docs.title: Design Lab: what it covers
docs.text: Design Lab. Interface design you can see and measure: styles, principles and the laws behind them. Good interface design is a set of choices you can learn to see. Every chapter here uses the same small live interface (a card, buttons, a switch, a slider, a text field and a nav bar) and restyles it, so you can compare skeuomorphism, flat, material, glass and more side by side. Then the principles that make any style work, and a handful of UX laws you can test on yourself, with your own reaction times.

docs.title: Design Lab: chapters
docs.text: Design Lab chapters. Skeuomorphism: Leather, stitching and glossy buttons: the real world, drawn. Flat design: Strip the texture, keep the colour. Fast, clean, and easy to get wrong. Material design: Paper and ink: elevation, shadows that mean something, ripples. Neumorphism: Soft UI pressed out of the background, and its contrast problem. Glassmorphism: Frosted panels over colour, and keeping text readable on them. Claymorphism: Puffy, pastel, friendly. Inner shadows doing the modelling. Brutalism: Raw HTML honesty and its loud cousin, neo-brutalism.

docs.title: Design Lab: chapters
docs.text: Minimalism and Swiss style: Less but better. Grids, type and one accent colour. Style morpher: Slide between every style and watch each property move. White space: Padding, line height and margins on a real layout. Visual hierarchy: Size, weight, colour and position. Squint to test it. Alignment and grids: A 12 column grid, snapping, and finding near misses. Gestalt principles: Why the eye groups dots: proximity, similarity, closure and more. Colour: HSL, harmony rules, 60-30-10 and WCAG contrast. Typography: Type scales, line length and pairing typefaces. Laws gallery: Jakob, Tesler, Doherty, aesthetics, isolation, serial position, peak-end.

docs.title: Study Lab: Physics
docs.text: Physics, a Study Lab subject. Motion, forces, energy, orbits, waves, light and gases as live simulations with graphs.

docs.title: Physics Lab: what it covers
docs.text: Physics Lab. Mechanics, waves and light, each one a live simulation you can push, drag and break. Physics is a small set of rules that predicts how things move, swing, ripple and shine. Every chapter here is a real simulation: the computer applies those rules many times a second, so what you see is the physics working, not a canned animation. Start at the top if physics is new to you, or jump to whatever you are curious about.

docs.title: Physics Lab: chapters
docs.text: Physics Lab chapters. Motion graphs: Drag a runner and watch position, velocity and acceleration draw themselves. Vectors: Arrows with size and direction. Add them, subtract them, split them. Projectile motion: Fire a cannon on Earth, the Moon or Mars, with or without air. Energy: A skate track you can reshape. Kinetic, potential and thermal energy. Momentum and collisions: Carts on an air track, from bouncy to sticky. Circular motion and orbits: Launch a satellite: circle, ellipse or escape. Pendulums and springs: Simple harmonic motion, damping, phase space and chaos. Waves: Rope waves, sound-like waves and a two source ripple tank. docs.title: Bio Lab: what it covers
docs.text: Bio Lab. Cells, DNA and the body's systems, one hands on model at a time. Built for pre-med study. Biology is chemistry that keeps itself going. Each chapter here is one mechanism you can run: tap the parts of a cell, read a gene into a protein, break a base and watch the protein change, fire a neuron, beat a heart and keep blood sugar steady. Start at the top if this is new, or jump to what you are revising.

docs.title: Bio Lab: chapters
docs.text: Bio Lab chapters. The cell: Tap the organelles of animal, plant and bacterial cells. DNA structure: A 3D double helix, base pairing and antiparallel strands. Replication: Helicase, leading and lagging strands, Okazaki fragments. Gene to protein: Transcribe to mRNA, then a ribosome reads the codons. Mutations: Edit one base and watch the protein change. Sickle cell. Cell division: Mitosis and meiosis, step by step, with chromosome counts. Genetics: Punnett squares, X-linked traits and simulated offspring. The heart: Chambers, valves, the cardiac cycle and a synced ECG.

docs.title: Bio Lab: chapters
docs.text: Blood and immunity: Blood cells, ABO and Rh matching, innate and adaptive defence. The action potential: A live Hodgkin Huxley neuron, ion channels and the synapse. Enzymes: Michaelis Menten, temperature, pH and inhibitors. Blood glucose: Insulin and glucagon feedback. Eat, exercise, compare diabetes.
